```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, out.width = "100%", dpi = 96)
has_ggplot2 <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
```

```{r setup}
library(bdhs)
```

This article covers tools that go beyond computing a single estimate:

* calibrated synthetic data that reproduce the official numbers;
* checks of data quality;
* tests of change over time;
* measures of inequality;
* decomposition of change;
* progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals.

Everything below runs on synthetic data or on the bundled official estimates.
With your own files from `bdhs_read()`, the same code gives real results.

## Synthetic data that match the official estimates

`bdhs_simulate()` produces files with the right structure but random values.
`bdhs_synthesize()` goes further. It calibrates the synthetic data so that
key indicators reproduce the official DHS estimates, nationally and by
division and residence. It uses only the published aggregates bundled with
the package, so the result contains no information about any real respondent
and can be shared freely.

```{r}
kr <- bdhs_synthesize(2022, "KR", scale = 0.3)
attr(kr, "bdhs_targets")
```

`bdhs_synthetic_fidelity()` compares each calibrated value with the official
one:

```{r}
fid <- bdhs_synthetic_fidelity(kr)
fid[fid$margin == "national", c("indicator", "official", "synthetic", "diff")]
summary(abs(fid$diff))
```

Analyses on synthetic data therefore produce realistic numbers:

```{r}
bdhs_estimate(kr, c("rh_del_facility", "rh_del_csection"), by = "v025")
```

Synthetic data are meant for teaching, testing code and sharing reproducible
examples. Only the calibrated indicators and margins match the real survey.
Associations between variables, and every variable that was not calibrated,
are artificial. Never draw substantive conclusions from synthetic data.

## Data quality

`bdhs_quality()` runs the standard DHS data-quality checks on whatever file
you give it:

* age heaping (Whipple and Myers indices);
* women shifted out of the eligible age range (ratios at ages 15 and 50);
* completeness of birth dates;
* births displaced out of the five-year window;
* heaping of age at death at 12 months;
* anthropometric quality (z-score SDs, flagged values, digit preference).

```{r}
pr <- bdhs_simulate(2022, "PR")
q <- bdhs_quality(pr)
q[q$check == "age_heaping", c("statistic", "group", "value", "interpretation")]
```

```{r, eval = has_ggplot2}
plot(q, type = "age")
```

On real data these checks are informative. In the BDHS, for example, men's
ages are heavily heaped on numbers ending in 0 and 5, and far fewer women are
recorded at age 50 than at 49.

## Is a change significant?

`bdhs_compare()` tests differences between rounds, which are independent
samples, or between groups within a round, using the full design-based
covariance:

```{r}
k14 <- bdhs_synthesize(2014, "KR", scale = 0.3, seed = 1)
k22 <- bdhs_synthesize(2022, "KR", scale = 0.3, seed = 2)
cmp <- bdhs_compare(k14, k22, indicators = "rh_del_csection")
cmp[, c("survey_1", "survey_2", "estimate_1", "estimate_2", "difference", "p_value", "annual_change")]
```

It warns you when division-level comparisons cross rounds with different
division layouts. Use the harmonized `division_trend6` for those.

## Inequality

`bdhs_inequality()` measures wealth-related inequality with design-based
standard errors:

* the rich-poor difference and ratio;
* the slope and relative indices of inequality (SII, RII);
* the concentration index, and Erreygers' corrected version for binary
  outcomes.

```{r}
bdhs_inequality(k22, "rh_del_csection", by = "v190")
```

The same measures can be computed from the official estimates by wealth
quintile, without any microdata:

```{r}
bdhs_inequality_official("rh_del_csection", survey = c(2004, 2022))
```

## Why did it change? Decomposition

`bdhs_decompose()` splits the change between two rounds into two parts: a
**composition** part, due to a different mix of people (for example, more
educated mothers), and a **within-group** part, due to change within each
group. It uses Kitagawa's method, with jackknife standard errors.

```{r}
h14 <- bdhs_harmonize(k14, vars = "mother_edu_level")
h22 <- bdhs_harmonize(k22, vars = "mother_edu_level")
dec <- bdhs_decompose(h14, h22, "rh_del_csection", by = "mother_edu_level", se = "none")
dec[dec$group == "All", c("component", "estimate", "percent")]
```

## Progress towards the SDGs

`bdhs_sdg()` tracks Bangladesh's progress towards SDG-related targets from the
official estimates. It reports the annual rate of change, the rate needed to
reach the 2030 target, and whether progress is on track.

```{r}
s <- bdhs_sdg()
s[, c("sdg", "name", "latest_value", "target", "aarc", "required_aarc", "on_track")]
```

```{r, eval = has_ggplot2, fig.height = 5}
plot(s)
```
